h1: The 7 Best Compact Countertop Microwaves for Tight Kitchens, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 compact microwaves from 0.6 to 0.9 cubic feet, compared on wattage, controls, inverter tech and everyday usability.
summary: The Toshiba 0.9 cu. ft. model is the best small microwave for most kitchens because it packs 900W into a compact case. The LG with Smart Inverter is the pick for even heating and delicate food, the Chefman is the quietest and most feature-rich 700W unit, and the Commercial Chef is the simple dial-controlled option with the lowest sticker.
intro: Most people shopping for a small microwave pick on footprint and then regret the wattage. A 0.7 cubic foot cabinet with 700 watts can look identical to a 900 watt one on the counter, yet it takes roughly a quarter longer to heat the same bowl, and every package instruction on your shelf was written for a stronger oven.

That tradeoff drives this ranking. We reviewed seven compact microwaves from their spec sheets and listings, comparing capacity, wattage, power levels, controls and extras such as inverter heating, child lock and eco mode. Anything that is not published for a model is left out rather than assumed.

products.name: TOSHIBA Microwave Oven
products.verdict: The best mix of cavity size and power: 0.9 cu. ft. and 900W without crossing into full-size territory.
products.description:
The Toshiba is a 0.9 cubic foot countertop model rated at 900 watts. That sits one step above the 0.7 cubic foot, 700 watt class that dominates compact microwaves, and it is the only unit here that pairs the larger cavity with the stronger magnetron under $100.

It wins because the usual compromise on small microwaves is speed. At 900 watts, label instructions written for 1000 watt ovens need only a small time bump, while the 700 watt models below need about a third more. The extra cavity room also lets a standard dinner plate turn without catching the walls. It ranks above the LG only because the LG is pricier and its main advantage, inverter heating, matters less for reheating than for defrosting.

Buy it if you want one compact microwave that does everything and you have a little extra counter space. Skip it if you are fitting a shelf or cabinet cutout, because 0.9 cu. ft. is the largest cavity in the group.
pros: Largest cavity among the budget models
products.idealFor: Small households that cook from frozen and packaged food.
products.skipIf: You must fit it into a tight shelf or cabinet.

products.name: LG Countertop Microwave (Smart Inverter, 0.9 cu. ft.)
products.verdict: Inverter power delivery heats leftovers more evenly than a standard on-off magnetron.
products.description:
This LG is a 0.9 cubic foot countertop microwave with Smart Inverter technology and the NeoChef label. The listed outside size is 18.75 by 14 by 10.69 inches, which is a manageable depth for a standard counter.

Inverter technology is the reason it ranks second. A conventional microwave reaches lower power settings by cycling the magnetron on and off, so a 30 percent defrost is really bursts of full power with gaps. An inverter holds a steady lower output, which is kinder to bread, fish, sauces and anything with a delicate edge. The tradeoff is cost: it sits in the $100 to $200 bracket, so you are paying for gentler heating rather than raw speed, and the Toshiba still wins on value.

Choose it if you reheat leftovers daily, defrost meat often, or melt chocolate and butter. Skip it if you mainly boil water and warm drinks, where an inverter earns very little.
pros: Even heating for leftovers and sauces
Compact outer size for the cavity
cons: Costs about twice the budget picks
Inverter gains are small for reheating
products.idealFor: Cooks who defrost and gently reheat more than they boil water.
products.skipIf: You want the lowest price or only warm drinks.

products.name: Chefman Countertop Microwave Oven 0.7 Cu. Ft.
products.verdict: Ten power levels, a mute button, eco mode and a child lock in a 0.7 cu. ft. body.
products.description:
The Chefman is a 0.7 cubic foot, 700 watt microwave that offers ten power levels alongside eco mode, a mute key and child lockout. For a microwave this size, that is the most thoughtful control layout in the group.

It places third because it fixes the small annoyances. Ten power levels let you simmer or soften rather than choose between full blast and a rough low setting, the mute button silences the beep for night cooking, and eco mode trims standby power. Against the Toshiba it is a clear step down in raw output, since 700 watts means longer cook times, and against the LG it has no inverter.

It suits apartments, bedrooms and shared kitchens where a late-night beep or a curious child is the real concern. Skip it if speed matters more than control.
pros: Ten power levels for finer control
products.idealFor: Bedrooms, shared flats and homes with young children.
products.skipIf: You want the fastest reheating possible.

products.name: COMFEE' Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: A 0.7 cu. ft., 700W workhorse with eco mode at a mid-pack price.
products.description:
The COMFEE' is a 0.7 cubic foot, 700 watt countertop microwave that adds an ECO mode to the standard preset layout. It is a middle-of-the-road unit in specs and price.

It ranks fourth because it does what a small microwave should without standing out. Compared with the Chefman, it lacks the stated power level count and mute function. Compared with the BLACK+DECKER below, the eco mode is its edge, since the display and standby draw can be reduced when the oven is idle, which adds up over a year in a kitchen where it sits unused most of the day.

Buy it if you want an unfussy, widely available 700 watt microwave and care about idle power use. Skip it if you want inverter heating or a full-size cavity, neither of which it offers.
pros: ECO mode reduces idle power use
products.idealFor: Buyers who want a plain, energy-aware 700W microwave.
products.skipIf: You want finer power control or faster heating.

products.name: BLACK+DECKER Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: A no-frills 0.7 cu. ft., 700W microwave from a name people already trust.
products.description:
The BLACK+DECKER is a 0.7 cubic foot, 700 watt countertop microwave. The listing gives little beyond capacity and wattage, which tells you it is a basic appliance with presets and a timer rather than a feature showcase.

It lands fifth because a brand name is not a spec. Next to the COMFEE' it has no stated eco mode, and next to the Chefman it lists no extra controls. What it offers is predictability: a 700 watt cabinet with a familiar footprint, and a manufacturer with a long history in small kitchen appliances, which counts when you need a replacement or a warranty claim.

It works for a dorm, office kitchenette or guest room where the oven is used for coffee, soup and leftovers. Skip it if you want child lock, mute or inverter heating.
products.idealFor: Offices, dorms and guest rooms with light use.
products.skipIf: You want child lock or advanced heating.

products.name: Farberware 0.7 Cu. Ft. Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: Auto cook, defrost and child lock make this a quietly practical 700W choice.
products.description:
The Farberware is a 0.7 cubic foot microwave with 700 watts, auto cook settings, a defrost function, an easy-clean interior and a child safety lock, in a black finish.

It ranks sixth because the preset features help beginners but the platform is basic. Auto cook buttons take the guesswork out of popcorn, potatoes and beverages, and a defrost function saves manual power math. The cons are the same as every 700 watt unit: slower cooking, and no power level count in the listing, so you cannot judge how fine the manual control is. It also sits behind the Chefman on child safety and noise control.

Buy it for a first apartment or a household member who prefers a button to a recipe. Skip it if you want to tune power levels yourself.
pros: Auto cook presets simplify daily tasks
products.idealFor: First apartments and users who like one-touch buttons.
products.skipIf: You want to tune power levels manually.

products.name: Commercial Chef 0.6 Cu. Ft. Countertop Microwave Oven
products.verdict: The smallest cavity here, with mechanical dials and a pull handle that skip the touchpad.
products.description:
The Commercial Chef is a 0.6 cubic foot, 700 watt microwave with mechanical dial controls, six power levels and a pull handle door. It has the smallest cavity in this ranking.

It finishes last on features but earns a niche. Dials do not fail the way touch membranes do, and they are easier for anyone who dislikes digital menus. The 0.6 cu. ft. cavity is also tighter than the 0.7 class, so wider plates and casserole dishes may not turn freely. Six power levels are enough for basic defrost and reheating.

It is the right choice for a very small kitchen, a workshop or an older household that wants dials. Skip it if you need a clock display, presets or an interior that fits larger dishes.
pros: Pull handle door is easy to grip
Six power levels for basic tasks
products.idealFor: Tiny kitchens and anyone who prefers simple dials.
products.skipIf: You want presets, a clock or larger dishes.

methodology.title: Wattage and cook speed
methodology.description: Rated output from 700W to 900W was compared against typical package times, since power drives how fast a small microwave actually heats.

methodology.title: Cavity capacity
methodology.description: Capacities of 0.6, 0.7 and 0.9 cubic feet were weighed against realistic plate and bowl sizes for single-person and small-household cooking.

methodology.title: Control design
methodology.description: Mechanical dials, preset buttons and power level counts were scored for how easy they are to use daily.

methodology.title: Heating technology
methodology.description: Inverter delivery was compared to standard on-off cycling, since it changes how even defrost and low-power cooking feel.

methodology.title: Extras and safety
methodology.description: Child lock, mute, eco mode and easy-clean interiors were considered as everyday conveniences rather than headline features.

whatMatters.detail: Wattage is the oven's maximum microwave output, and it decides how long food takes. Most package instructions assume 1000 to 1200 watts, so a 700 watt unit needs noticeably more time and may heat unevenly in the middle. Check the listing for the wattage figure, and treat 900W as the practical floor if you cook from frozen food.

A cavity of 0.6 to 0.9 cubic feet is small enough for a counter but can limit dish size. Standard dinner plates and wide casserole dishes tend to scrape the walls at the low end. Look for the cavity figure in cubic feet and check it against the diameter of your largest plate.

A standard microwave reaches a lower setting by cycling full power on and off, which can leave cold and hot spots. An inverter delivers a steadier lower output, which suits defrosting and delicate food. It costs more, so reserve it for cooks who defrost or reheat sauces regularly.

Mechanical dials are durable and simple, while touchpads offer presets and finer power steps. Ten power levels let you simmer or soften food; six is enough for defrost. Check whether the listing names the power level count, and prefer one that does.

A child lock disables the keypad so a toddler cannot start the oven. A mute button silences the end-of-cycle beep, which matters in studios and shared homes. Eco mode reduces standby draw. Look for these on the feature list rather than assuming they are included.

faq.q: Can a 700 watt microwave use package instructions?
faq.a: Yes, but you will need to add time. Most instructions are written for 1000 watt ovens, so a 700 watt unit often needs about a third more, and a 900 watt unit needs a small bump. Stir or rotate halfway through to avoid cold spots.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake with small microwaves?
faq.a: Choosing by footprint alone. Two models that look identical on the counter can differ by 200 watts, which changes cook times and results. Always check the wattage as well as the cubic-foot figure.

faq.q: Is an inverter microwave worth it over a standard one?
faq.a: Only if you defrost or reheat delicate food. For boiling water and warming drinks, a standard unit performs the same. The LG's inverter makes the most sense for cooks who thaw meat or melt chocolate regularly.

faq.q: How should I set one up in a small kitchen?
faq.a: Leave several inches of clearance above and beside the microwave for ventilation, and keep it on a stable, level surface. Plug it into its own outlet where possible, since small kitchens often overload shared circuits.

faq.q: How do I clean a microwave and keep it fresh?
faq.a: Heat a bowl of water with a slice of lemon for a couple of minutes, then wipe the steamed interior with a damp cloth. Remove the turntable occasionally and wash it by hand, and do not run the oven empty.

faq.q: Do mechanical dials make a microwave more reliable?
faq.a: They remove touchpad failures and are simple to operate, which is why the Commercial Chef appeals to people who want durability and simplicity. They do offer fewer presets and a tighter 0.6 cu. ft. cavity.

finalTake: The Toshiba is the pick for most kitchens because 900 watts at 0.9 cubic feet fixes the usual small-microwave problem of slow heating. Choose the LG for gentle, even defrosting, the Chefman for quiet and control, and the Commercial Chef when space and simplicity matter more than power. Avoid 700 watt models if you cook from frozen, because the longer times add up fast.
